Chapter Three: The Four Life Positions and Their Impact on Self and Others
Let’s dive into something that goes even deeper than the basic mechanics of ego states or transactions. Imagine the core beliefs you hold about yourself and the people around you—those quiet assumptions that color every interaction and choice you make. These are called life positions, and they’re like the emotional backdrop behind all your conversations and relationships.
There are four basic life positions. Each one is a unique mix of how you see yourself and how you see others. Let’s break them down together.
First, there’s “I’m Not OK – You’re OK.” Sound familiar? This is where most of us start, especially as kids. Maybe you learned it from critical adults, or grew up feeling a bit invisible. When you’re in this spot, you might find yourself needing approval, feeling anxious, or letting others take the lead—even when you have something important to say.
The second one is “I’m Not OK – You’re Not OK.” This one usually comes after disappointment or trauma, leading to a sense of hopelessness. It’s like believing that both you and everyone else are flawed or untrustworthy. People here often withdraw, become cynical, or just feel stuck in despair.
Third, there’s “I’m OK – You’re Not OK.” In this position, you might feel superior, or find yourself judging others harshly. It’s often a way to protect yourself from feeling not OK inside. But the cost? It can make you seem controlling or dismissive, closing off real connection.
And finally, there’s “I’m OK – You’re OK.” This is the sweet spot—the most balanced and healthy position. Here, you accept yourself and respect others, which opens the door for honest, constructive, and fulfilling relationships.
Now, these positions aren’t set in stone. You might notice yourself moving between them, depending on your mood, your environment, or who you’re talking with. But, most of us have a default position—a kind of emotional home base—that colors the way we see the world.
The real goal? It’s to move toward that “I’m OK – You’re OK” mindset. When you’re here, you show up with confidence, empathy, and resilience. Mistakes become chances to learn, and differences don’t scare you—they’re just part of life.
So, how do you actually get there? It takes some real self-awareness and a bit of work. You start by noticing those old patterns—catching yourself when a negative belief pops up. Then, you challenge those beliefs, and practice new, more supportive ways of thinking and relating.
Let’s look at a real-world example. Imagine you’re at work, and you feel “I’m Not OK – You’re OK.” Maybe you hold back on sharing your ideas, worried someone will shoot them down. But if you shift toward “I’m OK – You’re OK,” suddenly, you can contribute freely—knowing your perspective is just as valuable as anyone else’s.
This shows up at home, too. Take a parent who’s stuck in “I’m OK – You’re Not OK.” They might be overly critical, which slowly chips away at a child’s confidence. But when both parent and child move toward “I’m OK – You’re OK,” the whole relationship becomes warmer, more supportive, and so much healthier.
So what can you do to move toward that healthiest life position? Here are a few practical steps:
- Take a moment to notice which life position feels most familiar to you, and think about why that is. - Pay attention to moments when old beliefs about yourself—or about others—get triggered. - Practice self-acceptance, and try to offer that same respect to the people around you.
By understanding and shifting your life position, you can break free from those old, limiting patterns. And as you do, you’ll find your relationships—not just with others, but with yourself—becoming more genuine, more satisfying, and a whole lot more fulfilling.
